q: Does the stabilizer-frame simulator retain its exact chi = 2^t scaling and machine-precision fidelity when applied to structured magic-state distillation circuits (e.g. 15-to-1 or Bravyi-Haah protocols), where T-gates are placed on encoded qubits and interspersed with heavy Clifford postselection?
basis: This replication tested only unstructured Clifford-plus-random-T circuits at t <= 8. Magic-state distillation is the canonical near-Clifford application and features very different T-placement statistics (correlated T's on ancilla registers, followed by Clifford decode + measurement postselection) that may either (a) admit frame collapse via measurement conditioning, or (b) hit worst-case chi = 2^t with no cancellation. The paper does not test this regime directly.
next_steps: Encode a 15-to-1 distillation subroutine (n = 16 including one output qubit) as a Clifford + 15 T circuit, run the frame simulator, and check whether Pauli-measurement postselection on the syndrome qubits collapses chi below 2^15 or leaves it at the worst case. Compare distilled-state fidelity vs analytic ~1 - 35 p^3 formula. Free-endpoint feasible on m1 or uicgpu; no external cost.

q: Can a hybrid frame + tensor-network representation extend the useful T-count beyond the ~50-100 T regime where a pure 2^t frame becomes intractable?
basis: Frame cost is provably exponential in T (chi = 2^t under the standard rank-2 T decomposition). MPS-based simulators (e.g. quimb, ITensor) are efficient for low-entanglement states but exponential in the maximum bond dimension. Recent work (Kissinger, van de Wetering 2019; Koh et al. 2020) suggests hybrid encodings where each MPS bond is itself a small stabilizer decomposition, potentially giving cost poly(n) * poly(chi_MPS) * 2^{t_local}. The paper does not explore this hybridization.
next_steps: Implement a prototype where each frame branch is stored as an MPS (Qiskit's MPS simulator or quimb) rather than a Clifford-prefix statevector. Compare peak memory and wall-clock on QFT_n circuits at n = 16, t = 20 vs pure-frame (which needs 2^20 = 1M branches). Measure whether MPS truncation error stays below machine epsilon or introduces uncontrolled loss. All on free local hardware.

q: What is the achievable GPU speedup for the per-branch statevector rendering step, and does batched-branch execution (all chi Clifford circuits in parallel on GPU) shift the per-T-gate runtime constant enough to matter?
basis: Our measured per-T runtime constant is ~2.35x per T-gate (i.e. chi doubles + per-branch cost is amortized). The dominant cost at t = 8 is the chi = 256 per-branch Qiskit Statevector evaluations, each ~3 ms on CPU. GPU batching (via qiskit-aer with cuStateVec or cuQuantum SV1) should permit all 256 branches to render in a single kernel launch. The paper reports multithreaded speedups on CPU but no GPU numbers.
next_steps: Port the branch-render step to qiskit-aer's `AerSimulator(method='statevector', device='GPU')` with batching (or a custom CUDA/cuQuantum kernel). Measure per-T constant on an A100 (uicgpu, free) at n = 20, t in {8, 10, 12}. Expected: constant drops from ~2.4x to close to 2.0x per T, enabling t = 15-16 in seconds instead of minutes.

q: How well does the frame simulator integrate with a noisy magic-state estimator (e.g. Howard-Campbell magic monotone or Bravyi-Smith-Smolin stabilizer rank lower bound), and can noisy-T frame branches with reduced amplitude prune the frame in expectation?
basis: In fault-tolerant circuit compilation, T gates are consumed from injected noisy magic states with fidelity ~1 - p. Under a noise-tracking version of the frame decomposition, each split T branch acquires an additional amplitude factor tied to state fidelity; branches with amplitude below a truncation threshold epsilon could be dropped. The original paper is noise-free; whether such truncation is safe (bounded output-error) is untested.
next_steps: Extend the simulator with a T_noisy(p) primitive that applies the standard T + a small Y-error branch with weight sqrt(p). Prune branches whose |alpha_i|^2 < epsilon. On a t = 20 Clifford + noisy-T circuit at p = 1e-3, epsilon = 1e-6, measure whether output-statistic error stays bounded and how chi is reduced vs the exact 2^t. Compare against Bravyi-Smith-Smolin stabilizer-rank baseline where available. Free tools throughout.

q: Can the stabilizer-frame simulator classically estimate energy expectation values of VQE ansatze at scales that competitive with hardware-efficient QAOA/UCC compilers, when the ansatz is engineered to be near-Clifford (small number of non-Clifford variational rotations)?
basis: The paper's benchmarks (adder, QFT, FT circuits) are fixed-structure. VQE and hardware-efficient QAOA ansatze can be Clifford-decomposed into blocks separated by parametrized single-qubit rotations; if the number of non-Clifford rotations is small (near-Clifford ansatz design), the frame simulator gives poly(n) * 2^t evaluation of <psi|H|psi>. This is not tested by the paper and would compete with quantum-inspired classical VQE simulators.
next_steps: Encode a 12-qubit H2 or LiH UCCSD ansatz truncated to t < 12 non-Clifford rotations. Sweep the variational parameters via a classical optimizer, computing <H> via the frame simulator (sum |alpha_i alpha_j <phi_i|H|phi_j>| = polynomially many Pauli overlaps of stabilizer states). Compare converged energy vs FCI ground truth from PySCF (free). Report wall-clock per gradient evaluation vs Qiskit statevector VQE.
